summary: This unit teaches you to plan an organisation's needs: to start from its strategic and business plans; to forecast demand and workload; to assess current resources and find the gaps in people, skills, premises, equipment, ICT and money; to compare options and value for money; to cost and prioritise needs, build a business case and manage risk; and to monitor and review the plan.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. **Organisational needs planning** is deciding what an organisation will need, in people, skills, premises, equipment, technology, information and money, to deliver the services it has planned, and when it will need them. At Level 5 you prepare the plan for a unit or a whole ministry, agency, municipal corporation, hotel or business, and present it to senior management.

The aim is to **match resources to the services planned**. Needs planning that is guesswork leads to shortages, waste and rushed buying. Good planning uses evidence, tests the options and states its assumptions, so that decisions on the budget are fair and can be explained.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Use the strategic and business plans to decide what services, and therefore what resources, are needed.
Scan the environment, project workload and convert it into the staff and resources needed.
Assess what you have and the gap
List current resources, work out capacity and calculate the gap.
Weigh redeployment, recruitment, leasing, sharing, outsourcing and buying, using whole-life cost and value for money.
Cost each need, add contingency, and rank needs by legal duty, risk and service impact.
Build the case and manage risk
Prepare a business case, state assumptions and plan for uncertainty and emergencies.
Track approved needs, watch demand against the forecast and review the plan at least yearly.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** of scenario questions, with sums on growth, capacity, costs, payback and percentages.
A **written paper** with short answers (terms such as capacity, contingency, redeployment, gap analysis) and longer answers in full sentences.
**Practical tasks**: produce a needs plan with a forecast, gap analysis, options, costing and priorities for a made-up unit.

blocks.note: Always round up when you convert workload into people: 16.2 officers means 17, because 16 cannot do the work. Work every sum twice.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Starting point: plans and types of need

blocks.p: Needs exist to deliver the organisation's objectives and services. So the starting point is the **strategic plan and business (operational) plan**, not last year's budget, a supplier's catalogue or a list of what people would like. If the plan says the agency will offer more services online and cut waiting times for permits from 20 days to 10, the needs are extra processing staff, an online tracking system, training and perhaps accommodation.

head: Type
Examples
rows: Numbers of staff, posts, grades, shifts
Training, qualifications, new competences such as data analysis or inspection
Office space, storage, clinics, workshops, access for people with disabilities
Hardware, software, networks, data security, digital skills
Databases, case-management systems, records, research data
Operating and capital budgets, cash flow, reserves

ul: If the organisation plans to move most services online within three years, the needs that rise are **ICT systems, data security and digital skills**; paper filing cabinets and queue seating fall.
If a new law gives an agency inspection duties it has not had before, the plan must identify **trained inspectors with the right equipment**, not new logos or parking spaces.
Needs that serve a legal duty or safety (for example required fire equipment) come first.
Information is a need too, such as a case-management database to track applications.

flow: Start from the strategic and business plans
Prepare the business case and risks
Approve, include in the budget request, monitor and review

blocks.p: Time the work so that it is finished **before budget preparation**. Needs that are agreed in time can be included in the budget request; needs found afterwards may have to wait a year.

Work most closely with the **finance and HR units**, which can cost staffing and equipment needs, and with ICT, estates and procurement. Ask each unit head to submit needs on a simple template with evidence.

blocks.note: Keep draft plans confidential until they are approved for release. A draft that proposes closing a small office, for example, can cause alarm and harm if it spreads through social media or informal talk before a decision is made.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **PESTLE** analysis reviews political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors that will change demand over the next three to five years.

head: Factor
Examples for a municipal corporation planning markets and waste services
rows: National plans to modernise town centres; changes in funding after local elections
Growth or decline in trade and tourism; fuel prices; the corporation's own fee income
New housing schemes and population growth; shopping habits; expectations of clean, safe markets
Mobile payment of fees; route-planning software; recycling equipment
New rules on waste separation, safety at work and procurement
Flooding and hurricanes; drought; waste volumes and pollution

ul: **Trend analysis:** carry past figures forward, for example "cases have risen 5% a year, so expect 5% more".
**Known changes:** a new law, a new housing scheme, a new service that will add or reduce work.
**Consultation:** unit heads and front-line staff know what is coming.
**Scenarios:** low, expected and high demand, so the plan can cope with uncertainty.

blocks.p: Growth of a fixed percentage each year **compounds**: each year's growth is on the new figure.

head: Example
Working
rows: Demand 25,000 applications, growth 8% a year: next year
Demand 20,000, growth 10% a year for two years

blocks.p: Staff needed = forecast workload / output of one officer. **Round up.**

head: Example
Working
rows: Each officer handles 1,500 applications a year; forecast 33,000

blocks.p: If a new system is expected to raise each officer's output, include it: with a 20% rise, 1,800 becomes 1,800 x 1.2 = 2,160, and 29,160 / 2,160 = 13.5, so **14 officers**. Treat the productivity gain as an **assumption** and check it, because it may not arrive on time.

State every assumption behind the forecast: growth rates, productivity, dates of new systems, the budget. Then they **can be checked and updated** if circumstances change. A plan that hides its assumptions cannot be questioned or corrected.

blocks.note: A forecast is not a promise. Keep it simple, say how sure you are, and revisit it during the year.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Assessing resources and finding the gap

blocks.p: Before asking for anything new, prepare an **inventory** of the people, skills, premises, equipment, vehicles and ICT the unit already has, using the asset register, HR records and maintenance records. This shows what can be reused or redeployed before new items are bought. **Capacity** is the most work an organisation can handle with its present staff and equipment.

head: Resource
Questions to ask
rows: How many, in which grades? How many will retire, leave or be promoted? What skills?
Age, condition, maintenance cost, remaining life, spare capacity
Floor area, number of workstations, condition, lease end dates, access
Hardware age, software support, security, speed, capacity
Approved budget, likely changes, committed spending

blocks.p: A **gap analysis** compares the **resources needed with the resources available**. It is not a comparison of this year's budget with last year's, or salaries with those in private firms.

head: Example
Working
rows: An agency needs 22 officers; it has 18 now; 2 will retire
A unit of 40 staff will grow to 52; 8 m² per workstation
A unit of 45 staff will grow to 60; 9 m² per workstation
A unit has 30 staff and needs 36

blocks.note: Remember to take away people who will leave during the planning period, such as retirements. Forgetting them understates the gap.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Ask each unit head to submit needs with **evidence**: workload figures, waiting times, asset condition, incidents. If a unit head claims she needs eight more officers but gives no workload figures, ask for workload data and test the claim. Do not approve, refuse or halve it without analysis. A planner who guesses needs will not reflect real workloads and gaps.

For every need, write down the objective it supports. An objective to cut permit waiting times from 20 days to 10 supports extra processing staff and online tracking, not a new sofa for reception or a larger car park.
Consult staff, the facilities unit, service users and the community when planning something like a new clinic, not only the architect, the Minister's office or the equipment supplier.
A needs plan for public buildings must include **access for people with disabilities**, because public services must be open to everyone.

head: Option
When it suits
Points to check
rows: Workload has fallen in one unit and risen in another (for example after services moved online)
Skills, willingness, handover, effect on the quieter unit
Cost in a full year, time to recruit, grade, budget
Temporary or uncertain need, such as space for two years while a building is finished
Rent as a continuing cost; break clauses; suitability
Both need a facility only part of the time (for example a conference room used once a week)
Written agreement on use, cost and responsibility
A contractor can meet the standard at lower cost (for example cleaning)
Contract management, quality, public duties stay with the body

blocks.p: Consider options in this order for most needs: use what you have, share, hire or lease, then buy. Squeezing staff into corridors is not an option, and outsourcing does not mean handing over all responsibility.

The cheapest purchase price is not always the best buy. **Whole-life cost** adds the purchase price to the running costs over the life of the item: fuel, servicing, insurance, repairs, training and disposal, less any resale value. Running costs can exceed the price.

head: Example
Working
rows: Generator A: J$2,400,000 + J$300,000 a year. Generator B: J$3,200,000 + J$150,000 a year. Eight-year life
Vehicle A: J$6,500,000 + J$600,000 a year. Vehicle B: J$5,200,000 + J$950,000 a year. Six years

blocks.p: **Payback period** = cost / yearly saving. A scanning system costing J$2,100,000 that saves J$600,000 a year in staff time and storage repays its cost in 2,100,000 / 600,000 = **3.5 years**. Check that the saving is real and that the system lasts longer than the payback period.

**Value for money** is the best mix of quality, whole-life cost and fitness for purpose. It is not always the cheapest item, nor the most expensive, nor spending the whole budget before the year ends. Where fuel cost or emissions matter, compare fuel-efficient and electric models on whole-life cost.
Plan for the **end of the asset's life**: sell, recycle or scrap old vehicles, computers and furniture properly, and update the asset register. Disposal belongs in the whole-life cost.
If space is needed for two years, avoid a long lease that costs more than needed. Look for a shorter term or a break clause, or a lease linked to the date the permanent building opens.

sections.title: Costing, prioritising and the business case

head: Item
Working
rows: 6 laptops at J$145,000 and 2 printers at J$85,000
Six officers at J$3,200,000 a year, full year
The same six officers starting on 1 October; year ends 31 March (6 months)
19,200,000 x 6 / 12 = J$9,600,000 in this financial year (the full cost is felt next year)
5 officers at J$3,000,000, starting 1 January; year ends 31 March (3 months)

blocks.p: Always show both the **cost in this financial year** and the **full-year cost** of new posts, so the executive sees the true commitment.

A **contingency** is an extra amount, often a percentage, added to an estimate to cover costs that cannot be foreseen. Example: office fit-out of J$25,000,000 with 8% contingency: 25,000,000 x 0.08 = J$2,000,000; total **J$27,000,000**. Show the contingency separately and explain how it will be used.
When requests exceed the money, do not cut every request by the same percentage, fund in order of arrival or favour those who complain the loudest. Agree criteria first, then score or rank each need.

head: Criterion
Question
rows: Does the law or safety require it? (for example required fire equipment)
Does it support a strategic objective?
What happens to the public if it is not met?
What is the risk of not doing it?
Is it the best option for the cost?
Can it start and be spent in the year?

head: Category
Meaning
rows: Essential: legal, safety or the service cannot run without it
Important, but there is a workaround for a short time
Agreed to be left out for now

blocks.p: Example: requests total J$140,000,000 and J$98,000,000 is available. 98 / 140 x 100 = **70%** of requests can be funded. Rank and fund the must-haves first; decide which others can be funded and which deferred.

A unit head who inflates her request, expecting it to be cut, distorts priorities and starves real needs. Evidence requirements and challenge discussions discourage it. Likewise, stock held back to avoid a budget cut hides real position: report it accurately and redistribute.

head: Section
What it shows
rows: Need, preferred option, cost and decision required
The problem, the objective it supports, evidence
At least three, including "do nothing", with costs and benefits
What could go wrong and what is assumed
Who, when, how it will be bought or built

blocks.p: A business case for a new fleet of vehicles must include **need, options, costs, benefits and risks**. Colour and model preferences, drivers' families and promises that vehicles will never break down do not belong there.

No forecast is certain. State the assumptions, identify the main risks, judge **how likely** each is and **how serious** the effect, and plan a response. A plan that depends on a new office opening in January should have a **fallback**, such as extending the current lease, and should monitor progress. Assuming that the builder will finish on time is not a plan.
Jamaica faces hurricanes, floods, earthquakes, drought and disease outbreaks. Needs plans for services that must keep running should include:

ul: **Emergency supplies, standby staff rosters and back-up power.**
Protected records and ICT, with off-site back-up.
A **business continuity plan**: the plan for keeping key services running during and after a disaster.
A contingency budget for repairs.
Avoiding critical moves or installations at the height of the hurricane season (June to November).

blocks.p: A health centre planning for a dengue season might forecast the rise in patients and plan standby nurses, extra supplies and flexible space. Example: normal 400 patients a week; peak +30% = 520; each nurse sees 80 a week; 520 / 80 = 6.5, so plan for **7 nurses** at the peak.
Include approved needs in the budget request in time for the budget cycle. Reflect the approval in the business plan, with owners and dates.

flow: Set up a tracker of approved needs: owner, budget, date, measure
Owners update monthly: progress, spending, problems
Track demand figures against the forecast
Adjust the plan if the forecast is wrong

ul: If demand is 15% higher than forecast halfway through the year, **review the plan and adjust priorities or resources**. Do not wait for next year's plan, hide the figures or ask staff to work unpaid.
A measure for each need should show that it has been met: for example "six officers in post by 1 October" or "new vehicles in use in the western region".
Needs plans are reviewed **at least yearly and when major changes occur**, not only when the Minister changes, every ten years or after an audit finding.

blocks.p: Compare actual demand and use with the forecast, update the assumptions, record the lessons and use them in the next plan.

ul: explain the purpose of needs planning and why it starts from the strategic and business plans.
list the main types of organisational need.
use PESTLE and trend analysis to forecast demand, including compound growth.
convert workload into staff needed, rounding up, and allow for productivity changes.
state and test the assumptions behind a forecast.
prepare an inventory of resources and calculate capacity.
carry out a gap analysis that allows for retirements and growth.
ask for and test evidence from unit heads.
compare options: redeploy, recruit, lease, buy, share, outsource and remote working.
calculate whole-life cost and simple payback, and explain value for money.
cost needs, including part-year costs and contingency.
prioritise needs using agreed criteria and MoSCoW, and work out the percentage of requests that can be funded.
outline a business case.
plan for risk and emergencies, including a business continuity plan.
monitor approved needs and demand and review the plan at least yearly.

terms: Deciding what resources an organisation will need to deliver its planned services, and when.
The most work an organisation can handle with its present staff and equipment.
The amount of work, such as cases or applications, that a unit must handle in a period.
A comparison of the resources needed with the resources available.
A review of political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors.
A forecast that carries past figures forward.
Moving existing staff from one unit to another where they are more needed.
Paying an outside firm to provide a service instead of using the organisation's own staff.
Purchase price plus running costs over the life of an item.
The best mix of quality, whole-life cost and fitness for purpose.
An extra amount added to a cost estimate to cover costs that cannot be foreseen.
Must have, should have, could have, won't have this time.
A document setting out need, options, costs, benefits and risks for a decision.
The plan for keeping key services running during and after a disaster.
The final stage of an asset's life, when it is sold, recycled or scrapped.

c1.title: A regional licensing office
c1.text: A regional office of a government agency processed 25,000 licence applications this year. Demand is expected to grow by 8% a year. Each officer can process about 1,800 applications a year. The office has 14 officers, and 1 will retire during the next two years. A new online system is planned, which management expects to raise each officer's output by 20%.

c2.title: Space for a growing unit
c2.text: A unit of 45 staff in a ministry will grow to 60 within two years. The building has no spare space, and the ministry allows 9 m² per workstation. A landlord in the same town offers suitable space at J$1,800 per m² per month, on a five-year lease. The new ministry building is due in about two years but may be late.

c3.title: Generators and scanning
c3.text: A municipal corporation needs a standby generator for its main office. Generator A costs J$2,400,000 and J$300,000 a year to run and maintain; Generator B costs J$3,200,000 and J$150,000 a year. Both are expected to last eight years. The corporation also considers a document-scanning system costing J$2,100,000 that should save J$600,000 a year. The old generator is still on the asset register.

c4.title: Competing requests
c4.text: At a ministry, unit requests for next year total J$140,000,000 but J$98,000,000 is likely to be available. One request is for fire safety equipment required by law. Another asks for five new officers at J$3,000,000 each a year, starting on 1 January; the financial year ends on 31 March. An office fit-out is estimated at J$25,000,000, and the planning officer proposes an 8% contingency.

c5.title: A health centre in dengue season
c5.text: A health centre in St Thomas normally sees 400 patients a week. In dengue season demand rises by about 30%. Each nurse can see about 80 patients a week. The centre manager, Mr Orville Henry, asks for standby nurses and extra supplies. The finance unit asks him for evidence. A unit head at the same authority says she will hold back unused stock so that next year's budget is not cut.

questions.q: Applications rose from 20,000 three years ago to 25,000 this year. What is the percentage rise over the three years?
questions.why: The rise is 5,000 on a starting figure of 20,000: 5,000 / 20,000 x 100 = 25%. Percentage change is always worked out on the starting figure.

questions.q: Without the online system, how many officers are needed for 29,160 applications at 1,800 each?
questions.why: 29,160 / 1,800 = 16.2, which must be rounded up to 17, because 16 officers cannot do all the work.

questions.q: The office has 14 officers and 1 will retire. What is the staffing gap for 17 officers?
questions.why: Available = 14 - 1 = 13. Gap = 17 - 13 = 4. Forgetting the retirement would give a gap of 3.

questions.q: If the online system raises output by 20%, how many officers are needed for 29,160 applications?
questions.why: New output = 1,800 x 1.2 = 2,160. 29,160 / 2,160 = 13.5, rounded up to 14. The gain is an assumption, so check that the system arrives on time.

questions.q: How much extra floor area does the unit need for its new workstations?
o: 15 m²
540 m²
135 m²
60 m²
questions.why: Growth is 60 - 45 = 15 workstations. 15 x 9 m² = 135 m².

questions.q: What would be the yearly rent for 135 m² at J$1,800 per m² per month?
The space is needed for about two years, but the lease is for five. What should the ministry do?
o: Sign the five-year lease to secure the price
Buy the landlord's building for the long term
Reject leasing and squeeze staff into existing rooms
Try to negotiate a shorter term or a break clause
questions.why: A temporary need should not be met by paying for years of space that will not be used. A shorter term or break clause keeps the cost in line with the need.

questions.q: Why should the ministry also consider remote or flexible working for some staff?
o: It means the unit no longer needs to plan its other needs
It could reduce the extra space needed, and so the cost
It always costs less than leasing office space would
It removes the need to supervise those staff in future
questions.why: Options should be compared before a need is accepted. Flexible working may cut the space needed, but it has costs and risks, such as supervision and ICT.

questions.q: Over eight years, which generator costs less in total, and by how much?
o: Generator A, by J$800,000
Generator B, by J$900,000
Generator B, by J$400,000
Generator A, by J$400,000

questions.q: Which set of costs belongs in the whole-life cost of a generator?
o: Purchase, installation, fuel, servicing, repairs and disposal
The purchase price and the supplier's delivery date only
Fuel and servicing, but not the purchase price paid
The cost of the previous generator's purchase years ago
questions.why: Whole-life cost counts every cost over the item's life, from purchase to disposal. The past cost of the old machine is gone and does not affect the choice.

questions.q: The corporation wants the scanning system to repay its cost within three years. What yearly saving would be needed?
questions.why: J$2,100,000 / 3 years = J$700,000 a year. The expected saving of J$600,000 gives 3.5 years, so the target is not quite met.

questions.q: What should the plan include for the old generator when the new one arrives?
o: Leaving it in place and on the register as a spare machine
Disposal by sale, recycling or scrapping, and a register update
Giving it to a staff member without recording the transfer
Deleting it from the register and leaving it in a store room
questions.why: Disposal is the end of an asset's life. It must be planned, safe and recorded, so that the asset register remains accurate.

questions.q: What percentage of the J$140,000,000 requested can be funded from J$98,000,000?
questions.why: 98 / 140 x 100 = 70%. It is a funding ratio and not a reason to cut every request by 30%.

questions.q: How should the fire safety equipment required by law be classed under MoSCoW?
o: Must have
Should have
Could have
Won't have this time
questions.why: A legal and safety duty is essential, so it ranks as a must-have and is funded first.

questions.q: Which figures about the five new officers should the planning officer show the executive?
o: Only the cost this financial year, since that is the budget
Only the full-year cost, so that the budget looks larger
Neither, as posts are not part of the needs plan
The cost this financial year and the full-year cost
questions.why: Posts that start part-way through a year cost little at first but commit the body to the full amount later. The executive needs to see both figures.

questions.q: What is the total cost of the fit-out with the 8% contingency?
questions.why: 8% of J$25,000,000 = J$2,000,000. Total = J$27,000,000. The contingency is shown separately and its use explained.

questions.q: How many nurses are needed at the dengue peak?
questions.why: Peak demand = 400 x 1.3 = 520 patients a week. 520 / 80 = 6.5, rounded up to 7.

questions.q: The finance unit asks Mr Henry for evidence. Which evidence best supports the request?
o: Attendance records from previous dengue seasons, by week
The opinion of senior nurses that more staff are always useful
A list of the staff who would like extra hours of work
The number of nurses at other health centres in the parish
questions.why: Past records of demand by week show the size and timing of the peak and allow a forecast to be tested. Opinions and comparisons do not.

questions.q: The unit head will hold back unused stock so that next year's budget is not cut. What is the right response?
o: Accept her plan, since the stock will be used next year
Ask her to hide it in a different unit's store room
Cut her next budget by twice the value of the stock
Report the stock accurately and redistribute it where needed
questions.why: Holding back stock hides the true position and distorts needs. Accurate reporting allows resources to be used where they are needed.

questions.q: After the dengue season, what should the centre do with its plan?
o: File the plan away until the next dengue season starts
Compare actual demand with the forecast and update assumptions
Remove the standby arrangements, as they were not needed
Repeat the same forecast again the following year
questions.why: Needs planning is a cycle. Comparing outcomes with the forecast improves the next forecast, and lessons are recorded.
